The linoleum smelled like old coffee and regret. That was Ben’s first impression of the *Willow Creek Gazette*, and truthfully, not an entirely inaccurate one. He shifted the weight of his messenger bag, the strap digging into his shoulder, and tried to project an air of eager enthusiasm that he definitely didn’t feel. He was seventeen, fresh out of a decidedly un-journalistic high school, and currently staring at a reception desk manned by a woman whose expression suggested she’d been personally offended by the very concept of optimism.

Her name tag read “Doris,” and she didn’t look up as he cleared his throat. “Ben?” she finally grunted, without a hint of inflection. He nodded, feeling his cheeks flush slightly. “Placement kid? Mr. Henderson’s expecting you. Third door on the left. Don’t bother asking for directions. Just…go.” Doris returned to her crossword puzzle with the ferocity of a seasoned warrior defending her territory. 

He navigated the narrow corridor, dodging stacks of newspapers threatening to topple at the slightest provocation. The air grew thicker with the scent of newsprint and something vaguely musty, like forgotten dreams. The walls were plastered with faded photographs of local events – the Willow Creek Apple Festival from 1987, a blurry shot of the town’s baseball team winning a regional championship in ‘92, a particularly unflattering picture of the mayor at last year’s Founder’s Day parade. Each image seemed to whisper stories of a quieter, simpler time. 

The third door, predictably, was painted a depressing shade of beige. A sign taped to the glass proclaimed: “Mr. Henderson – Editor in Chief. Please Knock.” Ben straightened his posture, took a deep breath, and rapped tentatively on the wood. A gruff voice called out, “Come in!” 

Inside, the office was a chaotic swirl of papers, half-empty mugs, and overflowing ashtrays. Mr. Henderson, a man who appeared to have been carved from granite and perpetually shrouded in a cloud of cigarette smoke, was hunched over a desk piled high with documents. He didn’t look up when Ben entered, simply waved a dismissive hand in the general direction of a rickety chair. 

“You’re Ben, right?” he mumbled, without breaking his concentration. “Good. Don’t expect miracles. This isn’t some glamorous newsroom, kid. This is Willow Creek. We cover bake sales, zoning board meetings, and the occasional escaped goat. Don’t get any ideas about investigative journalism. Your job is to file, fetch coffee, and generally stay out of the way.” He finally looked up, his eyes squinting behind thick-rimmed glasses. “And don't even *think* about touching the good coffee. That's for me.”



Ben swallowed, a little intimidated but also strangely…intrigued. The *Willow Creek Gazette* wasn’t exactly what he’d pictured, but there was something undeniably…real about it. Something about the worn linoleum, the faded photographs, and the grumpy editor that suggested a history, a purpose. Maybe, just maybe, he could learn something here, even if it was just how to brew a decent cup of coffee.
